title: 为什么这位华盛顿州知名政客认为电子游戏可以成为「软实力」？
content:
Washington's secretary of state says video games are 'soft power'
Business
Console
PC
Interviews
Why does this prominent Washington state politician think video games can be 'soft power?'
Washington secretary of state Steve Hobbs pitched developers on the notion of video games as 'soft power' during SLICE and PAX West 2026.
Bryant Francis
,
Senior Editor
,
GameDeveloper.com
September 15, 2026
schedule
7 Min Read
Images by Mouse family and Siarhei via Adobe Stock.
At a Glance
Washington secretary of state Steve Hobbs praised video games as exemplifying "soft power" at SLICE and PAX West.
Soft power refers to a country's use of cultural and economic to influence other countries in lieu of military force.
Soft power can be a bridge between cultures—but what's the risk of it becoming a domineering force?
Washington state
Secretary of State
Steve Hobbs made the rounds during PAX West and Seattle Loves Indies and Creators Expo (SLICE) with a fascinating pitch for game developers: we know video games
are a driver of economic activity
—but what if they also can be used as a means of "
soft power
" in geopolitics?
This pitch may be something of a surprise to many developers used to discussing politics in games in through the lens of
artistic expression
, or as a
controversy-inviting third rail
that could offend
certain audiences
. To hear a politician walk up and praise your work as a geopolitical tool could be flattering or terrifying depending on your perspective.
To make this topic more complex, some
scholars
and activists characterize the pillars of cultural soft power as being more akin to
cultural imperialism
—an argument that may be quite compelling if you're from a country that is used to having foreign culture projected onto it, as opposed to doing the projecting.
Related:
What Washington State is doing to juice local game development
So how can developers unpack Hobbs' message and what it means for their own work? To explore that topic, it's worth digging into the history of soft power, and to view it in the context of its polar opposite: hard power.
Soft power promotes culture and commerce, hard power promotes conflict and coercion
We can thank scholar and former assistant secretary of defense for international security affairs
Joseph Nyes
for popularizing the phrase soft power. He coined the phrase in the 1980s and shared it with the world in a
1990 Foreign Policy article
. "A state may achieve the outcomes it prefers in world politics because other states want to follow it or have agreed to a situation that produces such effects," he wrote. "This second aspect of power—which occurs when one country gets other countries to want what it wants—might be called co-optive or soft power in contrast with the hard or command power of ordering others to do what it wants."
And just to be clear—"ordering" other countries is often executed at the barrel of a gun or by threat of economic sanction.
The
deployment of soft power
has become a topic of debate inside Washington DC and across the globe, with experts identifying it as a key tactic in
China's foreign policy strategy
. And inside the video game industry, analysts
have argued
that the Saudi Arabia Public Investment Fund's extensive video game investments represent a soft power campaign by the Saudi government.
At SLICE, Hobbs laid out this contrast through his own experience as a former US Army officer and current lieutenant colonel in the Army National Guard. He served in Kuwait and Iraq, and his kids have served overseas as well. If countries have good relations thanks to an exchange of culture and trade, families like his don't have to fear losing their loved ones on a battlefield thousands of miles away.
"Right now we are in global competition. It is another Cold War," he said. "That is one of the reasons why I love this creative industry. As someone who has served overseas and been in wars... I don't want to go war."
"If there's a way for you to reach hearts and minds through your games, to make this world a better place so people can understand one another, to create change through those countries that are restrictive—I think that's a good thing." He recalled a tale he heard from a member of the visiting
Games From Poland delegation
about how growing up in the Cold War under Soviet occupation, they listened to
Voice of America
radio broadcasts that shared American music and culture with a part of the world forbidden from accessing it.
Voice of America—and its projection of Western culture into Soviet states—is a perfect case study to examine Hobbs' pitch. It's been
praised
for promoting freedom and democracy around the globe, and
criticized
as operating as a lever for promoting the US government's agenda under the guise of independence. But if it's such an effective tool, why did the Trump Administration—which Hobbs took a few well-timed jabs at during his speech—
try to slash funding for the program
?
According to author, sociologist, and occasional
Game Developer contributor
Katherine Cross, it's because the Trump Administration has prioritized boosting hard power—military action such as
extrajudicial drone strikes in the Carribean
,
a coup d'etat in Venezuela
, and an
invasion of Iran
—at the expense of soft power. "We are living in a moment where the people in power in this country are deeply despising of many of the things that do make the US great," she explained in a conversation on the PAX show floor. "They are the people who
dismantled USAID
, they are the people dismantling the
Forest Service
or
NOAA
. They are degrading our research capabilities at the
NIH
and the
National Science Foundation
, and so on."
"They are also disdainful of our popular culture. These are the people who looked at Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey and said it's 'woke'...they cannot accept that the best things that the United States produces are that are peaceable, that are expressions of creativity, expressions of the best
knowledge-based professions
,
